Laguna Pueblo

Laguna, or Kawaik, encompasses distinct village communities. This starting path compares selected NPS historical context with the Pueblo’s own preservation-office account. It keeps contemporary community stewardship separate from outside mission and highway narratives.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Identity and homelands

Laguna, or Kawaik, is a Keres-speaking Pueblo nation west of Albuquerque, encompassing six villages.

Read the sources [1] National Park Service

02

Historical context

NPS connects the modern village’s establishment in 1699 with much older Kawaik presence and the upheavals of Spanish colonization and the Pueblo Revolt.

Read the sources [1] National Park Service

03

Living communities and further study

The Pueblo’s own history page provides a community counterpart to architectural and mission-focused institutional accounts.

Read the sources [2] Pueblo of Laguna

04

Older presence and later settlement changes

The NPS account distinguishes a much older Kawaik presence from the settlement changes associated with 1699 and identifies six villages. Its railway/highway perspective is useful context, but does not define the beginning of the people’s history or establish present boundaries.

Read the sources [1] National Park Service

05

Preservation described by the Pueblo

The Pueblo’s preservation office explains advising leadership, recording cultural resources, consultation and coordinating repatriation. These are public responsibilities described by the institution. Protected surveys and locations are not reproduced, and its plans for additional museum or language work should not be treated as completed projects.

Read the sources [3] Pueblo of Laguna

Pueblo of Laguna — selected villages, history and Route 66 account ↗

The NPS distinguishes a much older Kawaik presence from the settlement changes associated with 1699 and lists six named villages. Its transport-focused history is an outside institutional perspective.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual main body: six-village and Keres/Kawaik introduction; selected older presence versus 1699 settlement discussion; village development and Route 66 realignment paragraphs; final privacy/photography caution.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Normal HTTP200. Largest-community claims, precise archaeological dating, contemporary economic summaries, current event schedules and mission interiors not adopted. Underlying archaeology and records uninspected; no present land-boundary inference. No outreach or access bypass. Linked media, original records and additional collections were not automatically inspected or licensed.

Cultural Resources / Tribal Historic Preservation Program — selected public programme account ↗

The Pueblo explains its own preservation office’s advisory, recording, consultation and repatriation responsibilities. It gives a community institutional perspective without exposing protected inventories or treating plans as completed facilities.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual public Program Overview: mission, Scope of Work and Summary paragraphs on leadership advice, cultural surveys, interdepartmental work, consultation, repatriation and stated future ambitions.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Normal HTTP200. Individual advisors/staff, legal entitlements, survey locations, cultural inventories and underlying consultations not verified. No protected records or site coordinates reproduced. Hoped-for museum/language elements are not claimed as existing outcomes. No outreach or access bypass. Linked media, original records and additional collections were not automatically inspected or licensed.
